#6034. Giving Howard Lutnick His Due: China Is a Hard Problem

Why was Xi blocking the exported chips the Trump administration was willing to give him?

Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick, Chinese President Xi Jinping, and an Nvidia AI chip

Why wasn’t China taking the chips? The ones President Trump was willing to sell them — for a piece of the action, naturally. The ones Xi Jinping didn’t need to steal.

The question presents, for me, another valuable lesson in humility — in what Rich Lowry and I discussed on our podcast this week as the imperative of checking your premises when real-world events pose unexpected complications.

Andrew C. McCarthy is a senior fellow at National Review Institute, an NR contributing editor, and author of Ball of Collusion: The Plot to Rig an Election and Destroy a Presidency.

Analysis: Without U.S. Military Aid, Can Israel Afford So Many Wars?

Considering its long history, the hundreds of billions of dollars involved over decades, its growing controversy and symbol of the special bilateral relationship, U.S. aid to Israel came to an abrupt end this month with barely a whimper. Rather than being announced in a platitude-filled joint statement and with a roadmap for its gradual demise, the news that “by the end of this year, we won’t be paying Israel” emerged in an offhand remark by U.S. President Donald Trump seven minutes into an interview with Fox News on Nov. 3, the day of the midterm elections. It took three days for Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu to publicly confirm the news, which he did by way of a on X. Israeli officials, who had been expecting the aid to unwind gradually after 2028 (when the current framework agreement expires) were taken by complete surprise.

But none of that can conceal the fact that the aid program’s demise signals a major downgrade of U.S.-Israeli relations, one that is wholly an American initiative, not one of mutual consent as both Trump and Netanyahu presented it. Moreover, Israel is now losing a major component of U.S. ties at a moment when it is more politically and militarily dependent on the United States than at any time since the 1973 Yom Kippur War. And, even if Israel’s economy has become big enough to cover the country’s military spending, its current capacity to do so is being tested by a major rearmament drive and the continued pursuit of an aggressive military policy that began after Hamas’s attack on Oct. 7, 2023.

Considering its long history, the hundreds of billions of dollars involved over decades, its growing controversy and symbol of the special bilateral relationship, U.S. aid to Israel came to an abrupt end this month with barely a whimper. Rather than being announced in a platitude-filled joint statement and with a roadmap for its gradual demise, the news that “by the end of this year, we won’t be paying Israel” emerged in an offhand remark by U.S. President Donald Trump seven minutes into an interview with Fox News on Nov. 3, the day of the midterm elections. It took three days for Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu to publicly confirm the news, which he did by way of a on X. Israeli officials, who had been expecting the aid to unwind gradually after 2028 (when the current framework agreement expires) were taken by complete surprise.

But none of that can conceal the fact that the aid program’s demise signals a major downgrade of U.S.-Israeli relations, one that is wholly an American initiative, not one of mutual consent as both Trump and Netanyahu presented it. Moreover, Israel is now losing a major component of U.S. ties at a moment when it is more politically and militarily dependent on the United States than at any time since the 1973 Yom Kippur War. And, even if Israel’s economy has become big enough to cover the country’s military spending, its current capacity to do so is being tested by a major rearmament drive and the continued pursuit of an aggressive military policy that began after Hamas’s attack on Oct. 7, 2023.

Although it has had its ups and downs over the years, Israel long enjoined broad bipartisan support in Congress and in public opinion, certainly in comparison with the Palestinians, Israel’s main rival in the competition for American’s affections. That bipartisan consensus began to unravel 15 years ago under Netanyahu, who preferred the Republican Party and Christian evangelicals over Democrats and even the American Jewish community, whose liberal politics made it increasingly uncomfortable with Israeli policies.

Netanyahu’s alliance with the American right looked solid, but it crumbled in the wake of Hamas’s attack three years ago. The initial sympathy for Israel evaporated quickly as its offensive in Gaza proved unusually brutal and continued long after its military justification had run out. Not only did remaining support in the Democratic Party collapse, but Israel began losing the GOP, as well—starting at the far-right fringe of the MAGA movement and rapidly moving to the center, especially among younger Republicans. Israel’s role in convincing Trump to attack Iran earlier this year made it even more enemies across the political spectrum, as did the settler violence against Palestinians in the West Bank, which even succeeded in alienating many of Israel’s Christian supporters. A day after the midterm elections, U.S. Vice President JD Vance asserted that one of the four reasons Trump voters turned their backs on the GOP was that they wanted to “change our relationship to Israel.” Never one to mince words, Trump cited a “great dislike” for Israel as one reason for the Republicans’ defeat.

In both parties, the $3.8 billion in annual U.S. aid had served as a flash point for anti-Israel sentiment. Progressives saw it as taxpayer dollars going to fund what they called “genocide” in Gaza; for MAGA Republicans, it violated the principals of “America first” and of U.S. allies standing on their own two feet. Netanyahu and his religious-right government shrugged off these dangerous developments. The far-right ideology that drives his government all but precluded policy changes that might have stemmed the growing hostility.

In purely money terms, the loss of U.S. aid isn’t critical for Israel. The annual amount that Israel gets hasn’t changed much over the years, but the Israeli economy has grown more than 20-fold. Thus, 40 years ago, aid was equal to about 11 percent of Israeli GDP; today, it is about 0.6 percent. Moreover, under the current 10-year framework, nearly all the aid money is today spent in the United States, so if anything, it harms the Israeli arms industry by reserving a big chunk of Israeli procurement contracts for U.S. makers. However, that isn’t the whole story. Aid accounted for about a fifth of the Israeli defense budget before Oct. 7. If it is 10 percent or less today, then that’s only because Israeli military spending has since tripled.

It is a testament to the strength of the Israeli economy and to the government’s strong finances (not to mention a vast increase in U.S. financial aid at the height of the Gaza war) that the country has been able to sustain such a vast increase, which, at close to 8 percent of GDP, is among the highest in the world. But the situation cannot continue indefinitely. The shock of the Hamas attack has left Israel feeling vulnerable, if for no other reason than that the conflicts with Iran, Hezbollah, and Hamas have not ended in a decisive victory. Netanyahu therefore wants to remain at elevated levels for the next decade. That involves not only more people in uniform than before Oct. 7, but a massive arms buildup that will saddle the economy with one of the world’s highest defense burdens for years to come. The loss of U.S. aid will mean that even more of the cost will fall on Israeli taxpayers than the government had planned on.

As it became evident over the past year that Trump wanted to gradually end the aid program (at the same time that European countries were increasingly refusing to sell Israel military gear and the risk was growing that U.S. arms purchases would be constrained by an increasingly critical Congress), Netanyahu began marketing the emerging threat as an opportunity for Israel to pursue a more independent military course.

Voters gave U.S. lawmakers a mandate to do more than just cut aid.

Democrats feel they have a mandate to put conditions on U.S. support for Israel.

That independence, however, will come at a cost, entailing the creation of an economy geared more heavily than ever to arms production. Turning Israel into what the prime minister has called a “super Sparta” will not only force the economy to produce the kind of arms and components that it could get more cheaply abroad, but it won’t seriously reduce Israeli dependence. Israel is a major producer of cutting-edge weaponry, but its industrial base is too small to make everything it needs, whether it’s a fighter jet or all of the thousands of tiny components that go into one.

Netanyahu’s Sparta is no substitute for Israel maintaining strong relations with the United States and its other partners. But, far from making Israel more independent, Netanyahu has done the reverse. U.S. financial aid and ammunition were critical for sustaining what turned out to be a lengthy war and occupation in the Gaza Strip, and the two assaults on Iran would not have been possible without direct U.S. military intervention. Netanyahu’s ambitions to remake the Middle East are too big for Israel to undertake alone.

In addition, the United States is Israel’s biggest trade partner, is by far its main source of foreign investment, and provides Israel with diplomatic cover in the United Nations. And, if that is not enough, Israel has no backup alliances to compensate for deteriorating ties with the United States. Quite to the contrary, the prime minister has presided over a severe deterioration in relations with Europe to the point that Israel is contending with increasingly severe sanctions.

So, what lies ahead for bilateral ties? The end of aid marks a transition from relations predicated on broad domestic support in the United States for Israel—something akin to friendship—to a more transactional one based on mutual interests and the strategic value that each side brings to the table. That Israel will continue to need the United States in this new era is indisputable. The question is what Israel offers the United States, because it will now have to justify itself as an ally.

It is safe to say that intelligence-sharing and joint weapons development will remain valuable to Washington. But Israel’s previously important role as a force for regional stability has diminished. That is most evident in Syria, Lebanon, and Gaza, where, rather than helping Washington to bring at least a semblance of order and economic development, Israel has insisted on continuing to deploy troops in their respective territories and launch periodic attacks. It has rejected even tentative overtures by Syria and Lebanon to establish security arrangements and has blocked Trump’s effort to begin Gaza reconstruction. The White House has shown remarkable patience in the face of Israeli defiance, but that may no longer be the case now.

And if the United States does finally disengage from the Middle East—an increasingly likely prospect in the wake of the Iran war debacle and the U.S. midterm elections—Israel may become just another second-tier power of little interest to Washington and with no influence there. That is a change that Israel can ill-afford to let happen.

David E. Rosenberg is the economics editor and a columnist for the English edition of Haaretz and the author of Israel’s Technology Economy.

#6031. Iran resolution blocked in first war powers vote since midterms

Sen. Tim Kaine, D-Va., seen here at the Capitol on June 17, said additional war powers votes are under discussion for when Democrats control both chambers in the 120th Congress. (Bill Clark/CQ Roll Call)

The Senate rejected a resolution Thursday meant to rebuke President Donald Trump over the Iran war weeks after the midterm elections demonstrated the depth of public anger about the war and its effects on the U.S. economy.

Senators voted 48-51 against adopting the Iran war powers resolution that the House previously adopted in mid-September that would direct the president to withdraw U.S. forces from the war.

As they have previously with similar measures, GOP Sens. Susan Collins of Maine, Lisa Murkowski of Alaska and Rand Paul of Kentucky broke with their party to support the resolution, while Democratic Sen. John Fetterman of Pennsylvania broke with his party to oppose it. Departing GOP Sens. Thom Tillis of North Carolina and Bill Cassidy of Louisiana, who have at times voted in support of similar measures, this time voted against the resolution.

Even if the resolution was adopted in both chambers of Congress, it would be largely symbolic since, as a concurrent resolution, it would not go to the president for his signature.

But the vote afforded senators the opportunity to register their complaints about the war for the first time since Democrats routed Republicans in the midterm elections.

It also comes amid a larger debate within the Democratic Party on how best to fulfill their campaign promise of ending the war as they prepare to take control of Congress next year.

Democrats have become increasingly interested in trying to cut off funding for the war rather than continuing to hold war powers votes. But they are divided on whether to demand an immediate end to funding in the next government funding bill in December or to wait until they take power in January.

“When we have the gavels, we are contemplating other things, and we're actually contemplating things in connection with the CR discussion,” Sen. Tim Kaine, D-Va., told reporters Thursday in an apparent reference to the debate among Democrats.

As of Nov. 13, the war has cost at least $48.3 billion, up from $47 billion last month, the nominee to be Navy comptroller, Arthur Miller, told the Senate Armed Services Committee at his confirmation hearing Thursday.

As with previous estimates, the number Miller cited Thursday includes munitions, equipment replacement costs and operational costs but does not factor in the cost of damage to U.S. bases, which alone is likely to run in the billions.

Last week, a trio of Senate Democrats unveiled legislation to prohibit funding for offensive military operations in Iran that they said they intend to introduce as an amendment to the next government funding bill, which Congress will need to pass to avoid a government shutdown after Dec. 11.

On Thursday as the Senate voted on the war powers resolution, Sens. Tammy Duckworth, D-Ill., and Kirsten Gillibrand, D-N.Y., two of the sponsors of the proposed amendment, demanded it be included in the next funding bill.

“We’ve already tried tool after tool to get the president to rein in this conflict. Nine months in, defunding the war is the only way to force Trump to end it,” Duckworth, who vowed to vote against any continuing resolution that doesn’t include the amendment, said at a news conference.

Sen. Michael Bennet, D-Colo., unveiled his own proposed amendment Thursday to bar any future and previous funding from being used to “support directly or indirectly combat activities by United States personnel in or over Iran, or in Iranian territorial waters” unless specifically authorized by Congress.

His legislation is modeled off of language Congress passed in 1973 to cut off funding for the Nixon administration’s bombing campaign in Cambodia, Bennet’s office said in a news release.

“When we vote on short-term spending in the near future, we can fund the government and end this war. It is what the American people demand, and what they deserve,” Bennet said in a statement.

Meanwhile, the House is likely to vote again on a war powers resolution before year’s end.

“Before the lame duck’s over, I hope to enforce a war powers resolution vote, and it’ll be a chance for Republicans to say whether they did or didn’t get the message on Nov. 3,” Rep. Thomas Massie, R-Ky., said Thursday in a brief interview, referring to the date of the elections.

As with previous resolutions, Massie’s would direct the president to remove U.S. military units from hostilities against Iran unless specifically authorized by Congress or needed to defend against an imminent attack.

The resolution was filed Nov. 10, and under the 1973 War Powers Resolution, Massie can force a vote 15 calendar days after its introduction.

John M. Donnelly and Lauren Green contributed to this report.

#6029. America and China Are Trying to Alter Their Economic Bargain

Analysis: America and China Are Trying to Alter Their Economic Bargain

Create an FP account to save articles to read later.

Downloadable PDFs are a benefit of an FP subscription.

Contact us at [email protected] to learn about upgrade options, unlocking the ability to gift this article.

Get audio access with any FP subscription.

The United States and China are locked in a derisking race. After decades of actively entwining their economies, both are now trying to achieve a degree of separation between them. Neither side seeks at this point to decouple completely from its rival. Each is trying instead to alter the terms of their economic relationship, reducing their own vulnerability to leverage, coercion or attacks that could damage its long-term prosperity and security, while working to acquire advantages over its counterparty. This is a struggle for power, waged through trade, investment and technology development.

Today’s derisking race signals the failure of the third attempt by the United States to build an open, fully integrated world economy. At the end of the Cold War, as after the two world wars, American policymakers were motivated by a mix of pragmatism and principle. They believed that there were enormous gains to be had from trade with large and potentially fast-growing markets. But they also hoped to bring to fruition the liberal dream of a ‘one-world’ global trading system in which freer flows of goods, capital and people would promote peace and freedom, as well as prosperity.

The United States and China are locked in a derisking race. After decades of actively entwining their economies, both are now trying to achieve a degree of separation between them. Neither side seeks at this point to decouple completely from its rival. Each is trying instead to alter the terms of their economic relationship, reducing their own vulnerability to leverage, coercion or attacks that could damage its long-term prosperity and security, while working to acquire advantages over its counterparty. This is a struggle for power, waged through trade, investment and technology development.

Today’s derisking race signals the failure of the third attempt by the United States to build an open, fully integrated world economy. At the end of the Cold War, as after the two world wars, American policymakers were motivated by a mix of pragmatism and principle. They believed that there were enormous gains to be had from trade with large and potentially fast-growing markets. But they also hoped to bring to fruition the liberal dream of a ‘one-world’ global trading system in which freer flows of goods, capital and people would promote peace and freedom, as well as prosperity.

In 1919 America had the world’s biggest economy, but the international political system was still multipolar, with other great powers in both Europe and Asia. Although Woodrow Wilson tried to persuade the victors, and his own people, of the wisdom of lowering tariff barriers and creating an open global trading system, both at home and abroad he lacked the ability to compel others to accept his ideas. Once rebuffed, America drew back into isolationism and protectionism. With no nation willing and able to hold it together, in the 1930s the global economy split apart.

By 1945 the world had become bipolar, with the United States and the Soviet Union standing above all other nations—and America alone briefly accounting for as much as half of global GDP. American planners at first entertained hopes of reviving Wilson’s vision, but the onset of the Cold War soon forced them to abandon the idea. Instead of cooperating to create a single unified system, each superpower proceeded to build its own largely separate bloc. Organised along predominantly liberal, free-market lines, the American-led bloc was ultimately able to out-produce, out-innovate, and out-last its Communist opponent.

With the demise of its former rival, the United States finally seemed set to restructure the entire world economy into a unified trading system. America and its allies hoped in the process to encourage the domestic transformation of their former enemies, preparing them to become members in good standing of what would finally be a globe-spanning liberal order.

The main instrument of this strategy in the economic realm was the World Trade Organization, and its most important target was China. To gain entry to the WTO China was required to make detailed commitments that, if followed, would bring its economic policies into closer alignment with liberal principles of open markets, limited state intervention and freer trade.

Political change was expected to follow close on the heels of economic liberalisation. Increased reliance on markets would lead to rising prosperity and, as had already happened in Western Europe and parts of Asia, the members of an expanding middle class would demand political rights to go with their growing economic freedoms.

American strategists knew that drawing China more fully into an expanding world economy would enable it to accumulate power as well as wealth. But they were reassured by the conviction that prosperity would eventually bring democratisation, and by the knowledge that democracies had seldom gone to war with each other.

For their part, China’s rulers saw the West’s offers of engagement as a trap designed to bring about their own demise. Instead of succumbing to the charms of liberalism, they remained firmly committed to a mercantilist-Leninist governing philosophy, in which the primary purpose of economic activity is not to enhance the welfare of the Chinese people but to bolster the power of the Party and, through it, the nation.

Thus, even as it allowed greater play to market forces, the CCP regime took care to ensure its continued grip at home. And it approached the global economy as another domain of zero-sum struggle, one in which the aim was to strengthen China’s geopolitical position and gain advantage over its rivals.

For a time, the nation’s leaders believed they had little choice but to accept the dangers of increasing interdependence with the West. Once having obtained membership in the WTO, however, Beijing began to take steps to reduce its vulnerability to foreign pressure.

After the turn of the century this derisking strategy advanced along four parallel axes:

To guard against the possibility of being cut off from vitally needed imports of resources and raw materials, Chinese companies were directed to buy up more overseas mines, oil wells and agricultural land and to build a vast merchant fleet and an elaborate global network of roads, railways and ports to carry their output back home. To reduce exposure to Western tariffs or trade sanctions, Beijing sought new export markets in the global south. To blunt the impact of U.S. financial sanctions, it began to build alternative international payments systems. Finally, to lessen dependence on imported technology China launched a series of costly, high-profile technology development programs, began buying cutting-edge Western companies and initiated a campaign of industrial espionage of unprecedented scope and scale.

From the end of the Cold War until the mid-2010s, Washington continued to try to ease Beijing down the path towards economic liberalisation. Together with this persistence, however, there was mounting frustration over China’s trade and industrial policies and its evident failure to live up to the commitments it had made to gain entry to the WTO. As the Chinese economy grew and its level of technological sophistication advanced, these policies appeared to threaten the future prosperity and security of the United States and other industrial democracies.

China’s heavily subsidized exports were hollowing out portions of the American manufacturing base. Relatively easy access to Western companies and universities was helping to speed its technological advance. Its ongoing military buildup and more assertive foreign policy stance darkened perceptions of its intentions and began to make it appear less as a normal trading partner and more like a strategic rival and even a potential foe. Despite all of this, it was not until the very end of Barack Obama’s second term that China’s increasingly forceful efforts to strengthen its position finally began to provoke a meaningful response.

Washington’s belated answer to China’s mercantilist, power-maximising economic policies signalled the start of a two-sided derisking race. The American reaction came first in the form of the experimental and at times spasmodic initiatives of the first Trump administration and then the more coherent, but also limited and cautious approaches pursued by the Biden administration.

Neither Trump nor Biden sought to decouple completely from China, nor did either of them formally abandon the original, ambitious goal of creating an open global economy. Nevertheless, albeit with some hesitation, at least with respect to China the United States started to move away from a predominantly liberal approach to economic relations that emphasized the virtues of openness and the prospect of mutual benefits, towards one that increasingly prioritized power and the pursuit of relative advantage.

America’s derisking campaign comprised several interrelated lines of effort. Regardless of cost, it no longer seemed prudent to depend on a potentially hostile China for minerals, drugs, metals, and chemicals that might be needed in a war or national emergency. To reduce the dangers of dependence, the United States began to use tariffs to constrict imports and subsidies to cultivate alternative sources of supply.

Once seen as a benign byproduct of globalization, the pervasive presence of Chinese-made electronic components and hardware in America’s critical networks now appeared to pose unacceptable risks of espionage or sabotage. Dealing with the problem of penetration by removing these imported products and replacing them with reliable substitutes called for new laws and regulations to guide private companies and government agencies. Finally, slowing the transfer of sensitive technologies required imposing tighter controls on exports and on investment flows both to and from China.

Beijing has reacted to these developments by doubling down. Xi Jinping’s determination to stay the course is due in part to the fact that America’s tougher policies did not come as a surprise. Back in 2002, in the wake of China’s accession to the WTO and the 9/11 attacks, CCP strategists had concluded that they faced a “twenty-year period of strategic opportunity” during which they could grow strong without undue interference from Washington.

Eventually, however, the Americans would turn their attention back to China and, recognizing how much it had grown, they would try even harder to weaken and contain it. At that point Beijing would have no choice but to press ahead.

In the past five years, China has done more to increase security of supplies of food and raw materials, diminish its exposure to financial sanctions, and increase the relative importance of the developing countries as markets for its exports. Together with these defensive measures Beijing has begun to take more aggressive actions. Rather than implement reforms that might have reduced exports and lessened tensions with other nations, it has moved in the opposite direction: ratcheting up subsidies, expanding manufacturing capacity, and boosting exports that threaten to destroy others’ industries and leave them even more reliant on Chinese goods. Chinese firms are also working to dominate global supply chains for critical minerals and other industrial materials. The regime has successfully used the threat of export restrictions on rare earth minerals to pressure America and its democratic partners and is actively seeking to tighten its grip on other potential “chokepoints.”

The U.S. rejoinder to this intense and purposeful campaign has been mixed and less than fully coherent. Since his return to the White House Donald Trump has expanded on some of the policies that he set in motion during his first term, but he has also taken steps that threaten to undermine their effectiveness.

The second Trump administration has prohibited the importation of Chinese-made drones, robots, and internet routers that could be connected to U.S. telecommunications networks. But it has also ignored the law banning TikTok, a Chinese-controlled social media platform suspected of gathering sensitive information and spreading propaganda, instead negotiating a sale to one of Trump’s domestic political allies.

To lessen dependence on China, the administration has sought to work with other countries to develop alternative sources of critical minerals. At the same time, in hopes of reviving American industry, it has strained relations with its allies by imposing across-the-board tariffs on their exports, driving countries like Canada closer to Beijing. Finally, since returning to office, Trump has tightened certain restrictions on high tech exports to China while simultaneously loosening export controls on advanced semiconductors crucial to the development of artificial intelligence.

China’s course in the next stage of the derisking race seems set but America’s remains uncertain. The history of the past century suggests two alternative trajectories. Having failed once again to build a fully integrated global order, the United States may choose not only to distance itself from China but to adopt a posture of omni-directional protectionism and strict “America first” industrial policy as it did after World War I. This risks leaving America isolated as its former friends band together to protect themselves from its own predatory policies as well as China’s.

The aftermath of the Second World War suggests a preferable alternative. Instead of completely abandoning liberal economic principles, Americans could decide instead to narrow the circle in which they are applied to include only those nations that genuinely share and are prepared to defend them. It is only by pooling their resources and better integrating their markets that the advanced democracies can counter a challenge of unprecedented proportions.

This post appeared in FP's The Reading List newsletter. Sign up here.

Aaron L. Friedberg is a professor emeritus of politics and international affairs at Princeton University. His most recent book is The Derisking Race: China, America, and the Fragmentation of the Global Economy.

#6027. Van Hollen: Senate rules changes a matter for caucus to decide

Sen. Jeff Merkley, D-Ore. looks on as Sen. Chris Van Hollen, D-Md., during a press conference on Thursday. (Finn Gomez/Getty Images)

Sen. Chris Van Hollen, D-Md., endorsed a bipartisan plan Thursday to adopt new rules aimed at speeding up Senate procedures but stopped short of calling for abolishing the filibuster, laying down a marker on a key internal debate for Democrats as he positions himself to challenge Senate Minority Leader Charles E. Schumer, D-N.Y.

Van Hollen joined Sen. Jeff Merkley, D-Ore., at a press conference Thursday to express his support for a plan from Merkley and Sen. Steve Daines, R-Mont., to, among other changes, adopt a “talking filibuster,” requiring senators to continuously hold the floor if they seek to prevent a bill or nomination from moving forward.

Van Hollen went further to say that while his personal view is that the filibuster itself is “anti-democratic,” changes beyond what Merkley and Daines are proposing are a matter for further discussion.

“I’m in favor of filibuster reform,” Van Hollen said. “How and when we do that is a matter for the caucus to decide.”

The filibuster, a Senate tactic that effectively requires a 60-vote threshold to advance most legislation, has long been the subject of calls for change or outright abolition from members of both parties.

Other changes Merkley and Daines unveiled in October include eliminating cloture requirements for nominations and amendments, reducing post-cloture time for legislation, and introducing a new suspension process modeled after the House rules to allow bills with broad support to move quickly.

Merkley actually held two separate press conferences Thursday on his filibuster proposal, one with his Montana Republican co-sponsor and then later with Van Hollen, whose bid to become majority leader he has endorsed.

At the earlier appearance, Daines said that he thought the changes, if adopted, would “truly be a cultural change for the Senate” and lead to greater bipartisanship.

“We believe these reforms are appropriate no matter who is in the majority, no matter what the election outcomes were,” Daines said.

Daines also reiterated his view that implementing any rules changes would require 67 votes from the full chamber.

But Democrats have been debating whether to use their new majority in 2027 to change the rules on the first day of the session with 51 votes, or to eventually employ the so-called “nuclear option,” a series of procedural moves leading to a simple majority vote.

Democrats used that tool in 2013 to lower the voting threshold for advancing some presidential nominations with a simple majority, rather than 60 votes. A Republican majority followed in 2017 by extending that change to include Supreme Court nominations, and again in 2019 to reduce the number of hours between a cloture and final confirmation vote.

A spokesperson for Schumer declined to comment on Van Hollen’s endorsement of the Merkley-Daines plan.

Schumer has said he remains confident in his bid to remain party leader.

Van Hollen reiterated Thursday that his “momentum is growing,” after several senators-elect have thrown their support behind the Maryland Democrat.

“I think people recognize that if we're going to deliver on the big things that the American voters stood up for and voted for, you can't just go back to business as usual and status quo,” Van Hollen said.

#6026. The U.S. Tech Outage Wave, Explained

This issue is preventing our website from loading properly. Please review the following troubleshooting tips or contact us at [email protected].

Analysis: The U.S. Tech Outage Wave, Explained

Create an FP account to save articles to read later.

Downloadable PDFs are a benefit of an FP subscription.

Contact us at [email protected] to learn about upgrade options, unlocking the ability to gift this article.

Get audio access with any FP subscription.

A wave of tech outages in the U.S. federal government and private sector over the past week have made a lot of people understandably nervous. The outages affected commercial air travel, email, banking, and more—in some cases causing disruptions worldwide.

A global Microsoft outage that began last Thursday derailed a number of services that businesses, schools, and governments rely on. Then the U.S. Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) issued a rare nationwide ground stop on Friday leading to widespread flight cancellations and delays. Chase Bank, Bank of America, and Apple services also faced brief disruptions in recent days. And on Tuesday, some internal systems at the U.S. National Security Agency (NSA) went down.

A wave of tech outages in the U.S. federal government and private sector over the past week have made a lot of people understandably nervous. The outages affected commercial air travel, email, banking, and more—in some cases causing disruptions worldwide.

A global Microsoft outage that began last Thursday derailed a number of services that businesses, schools, and governments rely on. Then the U.S. Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) issued a rare nationwide ground stop on Friday leading to widespread flight cancellations and delays. Chase Bank, Bank of America, and Apple services also faced brief disruptions in recent days. And on Tuesday, some internal systems at the U.S. National Security Agency (NSA) went down.

Given the outages occurred on such a massive scale and in quick succession, questions have been raised as to whether they were a result of nefarious activities. But there is currently no evidence that the recent incidents were due to cyberattacks or that they were linked.

The Microsoft outage was the result of a combination of factors, including a “latent bug” from July that caused servers to become “overwhelmed and unresponsive,” Charles Lamanna, Microsoft’s executive vice president of Copilot, agents, and platform, said in a post on X. Lamanna said a “surge in load” and decreased server capacity had also contributed to the outage.

The FAA is still assessing what led to the ground stop, which lasted less than five hours, but a preliminary investigation indicated that the technical problem was caused by the installation of a router at a radio facility in Arkansas that may have flooded its communications network. A radar site in Amarillo, Texas, is also being looked at as part of the inquiry.

The short-lived Chase Bank outage on Monday, which led to issues with processing transactions and seemingly had a ripple effect that caused problems for customers at other banks, was the result of a “software bug in on-premise hardware systems,” the bank said in a post on X, adding that “there is no evidence this is cyber-related.” Apple said the outage it experienced on Tuesday, which lasted hours and disrupted the Apple Store and other services, was the result of an “internal update” and not due to a cyberattack.

The NSA disruption, which reportedly caused the agency’s internal communications network for highly classified information, NSANet, to go offline, had a similarly prosaic cause. “The National Security Agency experienced temporary degradation during scheduled routine maintenance,” the agency said in a statement. “While some internal systems were affected, mission-critical capabilities remain fully operational and our ability to defend national security continues. NSA’s infrastructure is designed with multiple layers of redundancy to maintain operations during planned maintenance or unexpected events.”

The Trump administration has acknowledged the unease the outages have caused among the public while emphasizing that there are currently no indications that any were tied to a cyberattack or coordinated by outside actors.

“I understand the timing of these incidents can raise questions, and it should. The American people should ask us these questions,” Director of National Intelligence Jay Clayton told the House Homeland Security Committee on Wednesday. “But based on what we know today, after a great deal of digital diligence, these are separate service outages associated with maintenance and technical changes. They are not a coordinated or state-sponsored attack.”

Secretary of State Marco Rubio on Tuesday recognized that people are “fearful” and “uncertain,” but he was unequivocal: “We are not under systemic attack,” he said. “These events—one has nothing to do with the other. They are not interrelated.”

But it makes sense that people are on edge about technology and how its dominance over modern life can make societies vulnerable. All of these incidents came on the heels of a series of suspected cyberattacks on supermarket freezers in Europe that caused millions of dollars in damage. They’ve also come at a time when anxiety over the rapid development of artificial intelligence has reached a fever pitch.

It doesn’t help that these outages hit as the increasingly symbiotic relationship between AI and the stock market was on many people’s minds amid the chaos swirling around Nvidia—following a salacious scandal that led to the resignation of the tech giant’s co-founder and CEO, Jensen Huang.

And national security and tech experts say AI may be partly to blame for these disruptions—though not in the way you might think. AI tools are increasingly helping organizations to identify vulnerabilities in their computer systems. That’s mostly a good thing because those flaws can then be fixed before any potential bad actors can exploit them. But those fixes don’t always go smoothly.

“AI code scanning has caused a tidal wave of vulnerability discovery,” and companies and government agencies are “rushing to make updates and fix” those vulnerabilities, David Agranovich, a director for intelligence on the National Security Council during the first Trump administration, said in a post on X. “[E]specially with legacy infrastructure, it can be incredibly hard to predict all of the different dependencies that might break because of those patches. The pace of manual patching has a cost, and that cost is reliability,” Agranovich added. “The result is many cascading and disparate system outages.”

Democratic Sen. Mark Warner, the vice chairman of the Senate Intelligence Committee and a co-chair of the Senate Cybersecurity Caucus, offered a similar assessment. Warner said in a statement on Tuesday that he understood why Americans were so concerned about the widespread outages and underscored that there is “no indication that these incidents are the result of a cyberattack, foreign interference, or some coordinated effort.” But he added that what appears to be happening is a “consequence of how quickly artificial intelligence is changing the cybersecurity landscape.”

AI has opened the door to “identify vulnerabilities across enormous numbers of systems at unprecedented speed, creating enormous pressure on companies and government agencies to patch those vulnerabilities immediately, often all at once, putting tremendous strain on systems that weren’t built to handle that pace of change,” Warner said.

The recent disruptions should serve as a “wake-up call” on the ways in which AI is “moving faster than our ability to manage its consequences,” Warner said, reiterating his call for “commonsense guardrails on AI and stronger cybersecurity protections.”

John Haltiwanger is a staff writer at Foreign Policy. Bluesky: @jchaltiwanger.bsky.social X: @jchaltiwanger

#6023. Xi Plays the Field at APEC Summit

This issue is preventing our website from loading properly. Please review the following troubleshooting tips or contact us at [email protected].

World Brief: Xi Plays the Field at APEC Summit

Create an FP account to save articles to read later.

Downloadable PDFs are a benefit of an FP subscription.

Contact us at [email protected] to learn about upgrade options, unlocking the ability to gift this article.

Welcome back to World Brief, where we’re looking at Chinese President Xi Jinping’s APEC agenda, an Iranian attack on a U.S. military base in Kuwait, and the European Union’s latest loan to Ukraine.

Chinese President Xi Jinping is just warming up for his highly anticipated trilateral summit with Russian President Vladimir Putin and U.S. President Donald Trump on Thursday. From delivering a pointed speech that criticized “unilateralism and protectionism” to breaking protocol with a big hug for Trump on the tarmac, Xi appears to be showing the world that he is eager to hold the diplomatic reins.

Welcome back to World Brief, where we’re looking at Chinese President Xi Jinping’s APEC agenda, an Iranian attack on a U.S. military base in Kuwait, and the European Union’s latest loan to Ukraine.

Chinese President Xi Jinping is just warming up for his highly anticipated trilateral summit with Russian President Vladimir Putin and U.S. President Donald Trump on Thursday. From delivering a pointed speech that criticized “unilateralism and protectionism” to breaking protocol with a big hug for Trump on the tarmac, Xi appears to be showing the world that he is eager to hold the diplomatic reins.

The Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) summit kicked off in the Chinese city of Shenzhen on Wednesday with a two-hour meeting between Xi and Putin. During the talks, Xi highlighted the importance of the China-Russia relationship and touted the necessity of a multipolar world.

In a keynote address later that day, he further vowed to defy trade protectionism and maintain a “free and open” system, painting Beijing as a stable economic partner that can counter the White House’s volatile tariff war. Putin echoed that message in his own speech while criticizing Western sanctions imposed on Russia due to its war against Ukraine.

The meetings and speeches did not signal a dramatic shift in policy; Xi has already used this week’s Asia-Pacific summitry to curry favor with some of the region’s most influential allies, from Canada to Peru. However, the timing was notable, as just a few hours after the Xi-Putin talks, Xi was on the tarmac at Shenzhen Baoan International Airport to personally greet Trump with a warm embrace.

Such a personal welcome is uncommon for the Chinese president, who usually sends a high-level representative to meet with foreign leaders when they touch down in China. However, the friendly greeting may be an effort to parallel Trump’s own approach to their relationship, as Trump met Xi at the bottom of the stairs to his jet when the latter flew to Washington in September.

Wednesday’s red-carpet welcome for the U.S. president also included an honor guard, a military flyover, an array of flowers, and a cheering crowd. Trump “loves pomp and circumstance, and these kinds of events present an incredible opportunity there,” Mike Kuiken, the vice chair of the U.S.-China Economic and Security Review Commission, told FP’s Rishi Iyengar ahead of Trump’s Asia trip. “[T]his is the kind of thing that plays to his insecurities in a way that he’ll very much enjoy,” Kuiken added.

Xi later hosted Putin, Trump, and the other gathered dignitaries at an APEC welcome banquet, during which the Chinese leader outlined the primary goals of the summit. “We will discuss steps to expand mutual openness, explore pathways to innovation-driven growth, extend opportunities for result-oriented cooperation across various fields, and strive to deliver more tangible results on the ground,” Xi said.

As for what will be on the agenda for Thursday’s trilateral meeting, Trump has stressed his interest in discussing the Russia-Ukraine and Iran wars as well as nuclear disarmament; however, experts expect Xi to try to steer the conversation away from nuclear arms collaboration.

Putin, meanwhile, appears optimistic about Thursday’s dialogue, insisting that the talks will likely have a significant impact on global affairs. “I therefore expect big potential benefit from the upcoming trilateral meeting,” Putin said.

Widening strikes. Iranian forces targeted a U.S. air base in Kuwait on Wednesday for the first time since September, upending a roughly two-month pause on strikes against U.S. military sites. That same day, Tehran also launched several attacks on Bahrain, which hosts the U.S. Navy’s Fifth Fleet. Both small Persian Gulf countries claimed to have intercepted Iran’s aerial assaults.

Wednesday’s strikes marked the latest round of tit-for-tat attacks between Iran and the United States. According to Iran’s military, the operation against Kuwait’s Ali Al Salem Air Base on Wednesday was in retaliation for a U.S. airstrike on Iran’s Qeshm Island the day before. Qeshm serves as a staging ground for Iranian forces targeting global shipping in the Strait of Hormuz, and it hosts an expansive underground tunnel network that is often used as a base of operations for the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps.

“If ​the enemy repeats its mistake,” Iranian Army chief Amir Hatami said in a video posted by state media on Wednesday, “we have the readiness and the plans to confront it and its supporters in a stronger, more crushing way and without geographic limitations.” Such a threat comes one day after seven U.S. officials told CNN that Tehran is considering detonating a so-called dirty bomb or chemical weapon inside Washington to target senior Trump administration officials. The White House has stressed that there is no imminent threat to the U.S. homeland.

Strapped for cash. The European Commission proposed a new $49.5 billion loan to Ukraine on Wednesday to help Kyiv avert its looming cash crisis and bolster its defenses against Russia. “We think this is the best way to give Ukraine a strong hand at the negotiating table,” European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen said. “And Ukraine only needs to repay once Russia pays for the damage it has caused in Ukraine.”

Last month, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky outlined a $76.8 billion funding gap for 2027, at a time when Russia has intensified its attacks on Ukraine’s critical energy infrastructure. Notably, Moscow is expected to double its drone deployments next year to 20 million units, which EU Defense Commissioner Andrius Kubilius said will likely force Kyiv to allocate some 62 percent of its military budget on drones.

A nearly $50 billion EU loan will cover roughly two-thirds of this gap; aid will be split between weapons funding and civilian needs, such as for hospitals and schools, and foreign allies will be encouraged to supply the rest. Von der Leyen expressed confidence on Wednesday that all 27 EU member states will support the loan. However, Bulgaria, the Czech Republic, Hungary, and Slovakia have already said that they will not take part in the latest funding round, prompting Germany to threaten to veto the bloc’s seven-year budget until all nations are on board.

AI cheating concerns. Around 550,000 South Korean students are preparing to take their university entrance exam, known as the Suneung, at more than 1,300 testing centers across the country on Thursday. The high-stress event is known for causing minor disruptions to businesses, as traffic is redirected, offices and tourist attractions open later, and extra trains run to accommodate test-taking.

However, this year’s exam will also include new restrictions to crack down on potential cheating after the top scorer of another professional test admitted on Sunday to using artificial intelligence to secure his suspiciously high score; the individual only got one question wrong on the tax accountant exam by using a miniature camera, a phone, and AI.

The admission prompted South Korean President Lee Jae-myung to convene an emergency cabinet meeting this week to discuss what the prime minister described as the “social evil” of AI-empowered fraud. “Cheating on exams using advanced equipment is no different from stealing the scores of hundreds of thousands of examinees who worked hard,” Lee wrote on X on Tuesday.

Among the new testing measures, all smartphones will be confiscated, glasses and watches will be inspected, and some public Wi-Fi spots will be blocked. A reward of at least 100 million won ($75,000) will also be given to anyone who reports an instance of cheating involving advanced equipment.

A packed week of high-stakes summitry has kept Trump busy and, perhaps, hungry. But Philippine President Ferdinand Marcos Jr. believes that he has the perfect solution. The host of this year’s Association of Southeast Asian Nations conference arranged for the U.S. president to receive a late-night delivery of Jollibee fried chicken on Wednesday as a sort of pick-me-up after a hard day’s work. Jollibee is the Philippines’s most popular fast-food chain and represents what Marcos described as a “taste of Manila.”

FP’s World Brief writer would like to note that she too has been kept busy and famished by this week’s onslaught of news and would also enjoy some Jollibee fried chicken if Marcos wants to put in a second order.

Alexandra Sharp is the World Brief writer at Foreign Policy. Bluesky: @alexandrassharp.bsky.social X: @AlexandraSSharp

#6022. GAO chief nominee triggers partisan clash at Senate hearing

Eric Ueland, nominee to be comptroller general, sits at the witness table for his confirmation hearing with the Senate Homeland Security and Governmental Affairs Committee on Thursday. (Bill Clark/CQ Roll Call)

Eric Ueland, President Donald Trump’s pick for comptroller general, promised to be independent and impartial if confirmed, amid criticism from Democrats and outside groups, during a confirmation hearing Thursday.

“I’m not here as a plant, a stooge, a lackey for anybody,” he told Senate Homeland Security and Governmental Affairs Chairman Rand Paul, R-Ky., after Democrats on the panel accused him of being a “rubber stamp” for the administration.

Democrats have criticized Ueland, a longtime GOP Senate aide and administration official during both Trump terms, saying he is too politically biased to lead the nonpartisan watchdog agency which conducts investigations and audits for Congress. They also said Republicans ignored a law that Democrats say requires the convening of a special legislative commission to make recommendations for the post.

Ueland said if the Senate confirms him to lead the Government Accountability Office, “We can at the end of the day ... see a GAO which is more effective, which provides better information for Congress in a quicker way so Congress is able to take policy actions and drive change itself at this end of Pennsylvania Avenue.”

At the root of the partisan clash is a suspicion by Democrats that Trump is trying to install a puppet to lead an agency that has fought the administration repeatedly over the power of the purse and other matters.

Democrats blasted Paul for rushing the hearing, which included a dozen other nominees for administration and judicial posts.

“It’s so apparent that this is a box-checking exercise,” said Sen. Gary Peters of Michigan, the ranking Democrat on the panel. “This committee is not doing due diligence, despite some of our members’ best efforts, because the chairman has chosen not to carry out his responsibility to provide advice and consent on nominations.”

Democrats said Paul did not allow Peters to make an opening statement at the hearing and restricted the amount of time given to senators to ask questions. A GOP aide disputed this, noting that Paul did not give an opening statement himself, Peters arrived late and all senators were given five minutes to ask questions.

Ueland has served as deputy director for management at the Office of Management and Budget under Russ Vought, the OMB director. Trump nominated Ueland to head the GAO, a legislative branch agency, Monday.

Democrats noted that the GAO has concluded multiple times that the administration violated the law by "impounding," or refusing to spend, appropriated funds. OMB has argued that the GAO misread the law and that it does not have any authority over the executive branch.

Peters told Ueland that the GAO had issued 12 reports accusing the administration of violating the law, and he asked if Ueland agreed.

“First, many of those items indicated by those reports, I have not participated in,” he said. Ueland said he had not reviewed the reports that Peters provided to him earlier, and that he would not offer an opinion on them.

He also said it was critical that he “not prejudge or come to this committee with informed conclusions about what it is that GAO has rendered as advice to Congress.” Ueland said he has a “clear commitment to follow the process.”

Peters said when Ueland appeared before the committee last year after being nominated for the OMB post, he voiced support for the presidential authority of impoundment.

“We’re going to expect you to continue to basically ignore Congress,” Peters said. “You’re going to be a rubber stamp for the administration.”

Ueland said his experience as deputy overseeing the management side of OMB would be a “value add to GAO.” He cited his work “examining how the government actually functions, how it is organized, how it can be better optimized to deliver results.”

Sen. Bernie Moreno, R-Ohio, asked Ueland how he would grade GAO’s work to date.

Ueland said he would give it a “medium grade over time.”

For example, he said GAO has 38 government operations on a “high-risk list … some of which have been on there for 36 years.”

By contrast, Ueland referred to his work at OMB, where he said “you have seen a very swift and aggressive effort by this administration in this term to set up systems and processes to ensure that we are not sending money out the door that we shouldn’t.”

Paul asked Ueland what he would do if administration officials told him they did not like a GAO investigation or conclusion.

Ueland said he would “fully follow through on charges from Congress and in the event of obstacles figure out ways to proceed to try to elicit information.” He said when he was a young staffer in the Senate, when there were disagreements between the legislative and executive branches, GAO and the administration had conversations “to see if there were appropriate paths forward.”

Responding to another question from Paul as to whether he would ignore a potential request from the White House to stop an investigation, Ueland said, “To be clear, yes.”

Sen. James Lankford, R-Okla., who is seeking to be the ranking Republican on the committee in the next Congress, said he was satisfied that Republicans followed the letter of the law requiring a commission to make recommendations to the president for comptroller general. He added that he was not “completely sure they have followed the entire spirit of the law.”

“For me, personally, Mr. Ueland is a great candidate in this role for GAO,” Lankford said.

Paul sent three recommendations for comptroller general, including Ueland, to the White House last week from the six Republican members of a 10-member bipartisan, bicameral commission. But he never convened the body to seek applications from and interview candidates for the post.

And he gave the four Democrats on the commission less than 24 hours’ notice last week to offer their recommendations. Democrats charged that Paul subverted the process, and they did not offer recommendations.

In a separate interview Wednesday, the president of the union that represents GAO employees decried the decision not to follow the commission process that characterized past comptroller general nominations.

“We see that bipartisan process as extremely important to preserving and keeping the trust that GAO has with the entire Congress,” said Benjamin Emmel, president of Local 1921 of the International Federation of Professionals and Technical Engineers.

Emmel, a senior analyst at GAO, said by sidestepping that procedure, “there is a cloud that hangs above any nominee where one party dominates that process.”

He said GAO’s credibility depends on members of both parties trusting that the organization is “nonpartisan, objective, independent and fair. If we lose that ability, we become less useful.”

The union is not advocating for or against Ueland or any nominee for the office. The Homeland Security panel is not expected to vote on the nominations until after Thanksgiving.

#6021. The Luxury of Children

Since its founding in 1922, Foreign Affairs has been the leading forum for serious discussion of American foreign policy and global affairs. The magazine has featured contributions from many leading international affairs experts.

JESÚS FERNÁNDEZ-VILLAVERDE is Howard Marks Presidential Professor of Economics at the University of Pennsylvania. This piece is adapted from “Terra Incognita: The Economics of a Shrinking World,” co-authored with Patrick Norrick and forthcoming in the 2027 Annual Review of Economics.

Why the Baby Bust Is Making the World More Unequal

The world’s fertility crisis is more severe than is commonly understood. Last year, humanity’s total fertility level dropped below what demographers call the replacement rate—that is, the average number of children that a woman must have to keep a population constant over the long run. This has never happened before. There have been periods when the human population declined because of wars or epidemics, such as the Black Death, in the fourteenth century, or the diseases brought by Europeans to the Americas in the fifteenth and sixteenth centuries. But now, simply as a function of their choices, humans will see the world population peak around 2055 and then begin to fall.

The story of the coming decades is not simply one of dwindling and aging. There is a great deal of variation in the baby bust. The most surprising trend may be one that has overturned basic assumptions about fertility rates. Where once it was thought that people—and, by extension, countries—with higher levels of income and education would have lower fertility rates than those who were poorer and less educated, the inverse is increasingly true. Many wealthier people and countries boast higher fertility rates than many poor people and countries.

The inversion is revealing of why governments have had a hard time coming to grips with the fertility crash. The best explanation for why people are no longer having babies is that child-rearing at the scale necessary to maintain populations is fundamentally at odds with the structures of modern life and modern societies. Once an economic necessity, children are now an economic luxury. That portends a world in which economic inequality is accentuated by demographic inequality, with widening fissures within countries and among them. The whole world is grappling with a decline in fertility, but in many different ways. And those differences will stoke further divisions, tensions, and even conflict.

Humanity falling below replacement has passed largely unnoticed. The central projections in the latest release of the United Nations World Population Prospects (in 2024), known as the report’s “medium variant,” still places the world’s total fertility rate slightly above replacement in 2026 and expects the global population to peak as late as 2084. But this medium variant does not fully incorporate the recent drops in births recorded by national statistical agencies, and its projections for future fertility rest on questionable assumptions, including forecasting a strong recovery of fertility rates in countries such as China. By comparison, the report’s “low variant” (the forecast that takes a more pessimistic view of future fertility) accords nearly exactly with my own assessment, which reflects more recent national statistics and takes a less optimistic view on the possible recovery of fertility. In that reading, the world has dropped below replacement fertility levels (approximately 2.2 children per woman) and will only keep dropping.

Fertility rates are plunging so fast that they are overturning many assumptions about demography. The steepest fertility declines have occurred in unexpected countries. Consider this test. Pick the state with the highest fertility rate among the following: Argentina, Brazil, Chile, Colombia, Jamaica, Iran, Malaysia, Thailand, Tunisia, Turkey, Sri Lanka, and the United States.

The United States, the wealthiest of the 12, has the highest fertility rate. This holds true even when just assessing the fertility rate of mothers born in the United States (immigrant mothers have a slightly higher fertility rate than native mothers). Dozens of other middle-income countries now have fertility levels below that of the United States.

That trend runs against the old explanation for demographic change, which held that fertility invariably falls as a community or society gets richer. That is demonstrably no longer the case. Among the countries in the Organization for Economic Cooperation and Development (OECD), richer members tend to have higher fertility rates than do poorer ones, even after controlling for migration flows. Take Mexico. According to the most recent survey, in 2024, a Mexican woman could expect to have 1.2 children over her lifetime, well below the 1.57 average of non-Hispanic white women in the United States. Mexico’s income per capita is only about 28 percent of the U.S. level. And just two decades ago, fertility rates in Mexico were much higher than those in the United States.

This dynamic obtains not just among countries but also within them. Richer and more educated households in the United States and other advanced economies now tend to have more children than poorer and less educated ones, reversing a pattern that had held for centuries.

There is no single, simple answer for why this has happened. Most theories do not hold up against international evidence. Factors that seem to contribute to lower fertility in the United States, for instance, such as higher housing prices, don’t seem to matter elsewhere, as many countries have seen even steeper fertility declines without skyrocketing housing prices.

Or take another favorite culprit, smartphones. Some researchers have suggested that the spread of the smartphone stoked atomization and a desire for individual fulfillment, discouraging many people from having children. But fertility rates have been plunging worldwide since the late 1960s, well before smartphones appeared, and there is little evidence of an acceleration in the drop after their introduction. Instead, the device is more likely an accelerator of underlying mechanisms than a cause in itself: by my calculations, smartphones compressed into ten years a change in fertility that would have occurred anyway over 25.

Another common explanation for drops in fertility is the spread of female education and employment. Freed from the domestic function of birthing and raising babies, the argument goes, women have chosen to prioritize other goals instead of child rearing. Although that shift may indeed have played a role in the twentieth century in lowering fertility rates, it is no longer so clearly causal today. Indeed, across OECD countries, the correlation between fertility, on the one hand, and female education and employment, on the other, is positive: the countries where women are more educated and more likely to work outside the home are also the countries with higher fertility rates. And in other regions for which demographers have good vital statistics, such as Latin America, the women not having children in 2026 are the least educated and the ones most likely to not be part of the workforce.

In the absence of neat, definitive explanations, a broader explanation for the global fertility crash comes into view. As societies embrace what is often termed “modernity,” they become incapable of maintaining replacement-level fertility rates. Modernity describes how countries have organized contemporary life around formal institutions (such as schools, universities, and health systems), specialized expertise (through degree accreditation, standardized exams, and professional licensing), and large-scale systems of coordination (such as multinational corporations, governments, and global supply chains). It is not synonymous with capitalism; communist countries, too, invested heavily in mass education and bureaucracies (and saw concomitant declines in fertility). The only way to run large, complex societies that harness modern technology at scale is to standardize knowledge and detach it from local custom through mass education, systems of expertise, and bureaucracies.

Modernity raises the cost of children and lowers the cost of childlessness. Parents must equip children with formal knowledge and credentials, an endeavor that takes decades of effort and spending. Tight career schedules also conflict with parents’ biological clocks. The most productive years for a research economist, for example, are usually between 30 and 45. Those are also the years when one needs to spend the most time with children. No matter how much accommodation a university offers, the day still has only 24 hours. Even when a researcher manages to produce both a large family and strong academic output, one can always wonder how much more that researcher would have produced with a smaller family.

And modernity has also made it easier not to have children. In traditional agrarian and artisan economies, children were useful factors of production, helping in the fields and workshops. Children also provided parents and other older relatives with eldercare. But the modern organization of economic life no longer requires children to perform those roles and the advent of welfare states has given the elderly other forms of support. Lineage once determined people’s present and future; it no longer does so in such a comprehensive way.

There are some exceptions to this seemingly universal trend. Tight-knit religious communities, such as the ultra-Orthodox in Israel and the Amish in the United States, have managed to maintain high fertility rates well above replacement level. But these groups have also stayed apart from much of modern life. For example, the Amish live in rural areas, where housing is much cheaper, and they end formal education at eighth grade, which eliminates one of the main costs of raising a child in a modern society, advanced education.

Apart from these idiosyncratic pockets, modernity has spread around the planet, with fertility falling everywhere. But rates are tumbling unevenly. In 1980, the richer an OECD country, the fewer children its women had. By 2000, the opposite was beginning to become true. The same reversal shows up inside countries. In Sweden, the demographer Martin Kolk has found that in every cohort born between 1940 and 1970, men with higher lifetime incomes have more children, and that among women born since the 1960s, the poorest have the fewest children. In the United States, the economists Moshe Hazan and Hosny Zoabi have found that in the first decade of the twenty-first century, women with a graduate degree had about 2.0 children, significantly more than the 1.8 for women who stopped at a bachelor’s degree.

Many adults still want to have children and flourishing families. When Gallup asked Americans about their ideal number of children in July 2025, the average answer was 2.7, a figure that has barely changed since the 1970s. But children are costly and bring no income. They have become something of a luxury good that richer people can afford more of than poorer people can. In the same way that a richer household owns, on average, a more expensive car than a poorer one, it also has more children—at least since the 1990s. Prosperous parents can hire help at home, order prepared meals, pay for premium grocery delivery or laundry services, and afford tuition and tutoring.

Richer families (and, among them, the most educated parents) also have more stable family lives. For instance, among Americans born between 1957 and 1964 (a cohort whose adult lives can be observed almost in full), about half of men with a high school diploma but no college education had seen their first marriage end in divorce by age 55, compared with 27 percent of men with a bachelor’s degree or more. Stable families lead to higher fertility (and much better outcomes for the children). In short, income and education soften some of the worst consequences of modernity. The intuition of this result applies, as well, to countries as a whole: richer countries can, on average, afford more “luxuries,” including children, than poorer countries.

If the modernity conjecture is right, the flip in the correlation between income and fertility that is evident within OECD countries will extend to all other countries over the next few decades. This is already happening in the Americas: among countries with at least 20 million inhabitants, the United States has the highest fertility rate in the hemisphere, well ahead of Argentina, Brazil, Canada, Colombia, and Mexico, and matched only by Peru, whose fertility rate is plummeting fast. (Venezuela’s official fertility rate is pure fiction.)

The same phenomenon will occur in sub-Saharan Africa over the next few decades. It is often projected that the continent’s high fertility rates will make up for shortfalls elsewhere—but that will likely not happen. Indeed, in those sub-Saharan African countries for which demographers have slightly better statistical data, fertility rates are dropping very quickly. For example, a recent household survey in the Republic of Congo has shown a decrease in fertility from 5.1 children per woman in 2011–12 to 3.5 in 2025. Similar falls are happening elsewhere and likely to accelerate as sub-Saharan Africa succumbs to the same factors that have sped fertility declines elsewhere.

The coming years will produce deep changes in populations within countries and across countries. The already sharp divide between regions and social groups with higher average incomes and education levels and those with lower average incomes and education levels will grow more pronounced, with the added dimension of contrasting fertility rates. The school district of a wealthy suburb outside a major East Coast city may not need to grapple with the widespread school closings that urban districts are already experiencing. And since political power in a democracy follows, at least to some extent, the number of voters, these different regions and social groups will see their relative influence in American politics change: New York, for instance, has lost 19 votes in the electoral college since the 1940s.

Something similar can happen among countries. In 1972, nearly eight times as many children were born in China as in the United States. In 2025, that figure has dropped to 2.2 times as many. China’s total fertility rate in 2025 was 0.93, while the U.S. rate was 1.58. If fertility rates remain at those levels, the United States will overtake China in annual births at some point in the 2080s and in total population by around 2120. That date might arrive earlier if the gap between the fertility rates of China and the United States continues to widen.

Demography is not necessarily destiny, but a world in which the United States has a larger population than China is very different from the world today. The shrinking and aging of populations will have first-order effects on a country’s economic performance. In research with Gustavo Ventura and Wen Yao, I have documented that nearly all of Japan’s poor economic performance relative to the United States since 1990 can be explained by its worse demographics, not by financial crises or poor economic policy. Among the great powers, the United States is the least exposed to demographic headwinds. Younger populations tend to be more innovative and less reliant on public support, a fact that bodes well for American prospects in the competition to come.

But for most other countries, demographic decline will produce significant problems. Aging Japan, for instance, is likely the best-case scenario for countries reaching a demographic sunset. It boasts a capable state and a homogeneous society with a high degree of consensus. More important, Japan became rich before it got old. Countries such as Mexico and Thailand, which lack many of Japan’s advantages, may struggle to weather the same demographic headwinds. While rich economies can rely on immigration to soften some of the effects of falling fertility, countries such as Tunisia or Bolivia, which lose many people to emigration, may find it harder to deal with their own baby busts. The new dynamics of fertility augur a world in which gaps between the haves and the have-nots grow even wider, as poorer countries and communities endure strains that wealthier countries and communities manage to escape.

Short of an unlikely turn to the social mores of deeply conservative and ideological communities, such as the Amish, only transformations in material circumstances will help raise fertility rates. Governments have had a hard time determining how to tackle fertility decline. Policy can do only so much in convincing people to make the monumental decision to have children. But that does not mean that governments should not try to reverse these trends. Their policies should respect the freedom of citizens to form the families they believe are best for them. Ultralow fertility seems to be caused not by a lack of desire for children but by the absence of the conditions that would make having children easier, or even possible.

In this vein, some policies are no-brainers. Governments should make education systems more accessible and less competitive than, for example, the ones found in East Asia and in the United States, where high levels of cost and stress discourage having children. They should build more affordable housing and provide more affordable childcare. Such material changes may have only a marginal impact on rates, but even, for instance, raising the U.S. total fertility rate to 1.7 from the current 1.58 would produce a significant impact. Fertility rates behave like the rates of return on a retirement fund: small yearly differences accumulate into large differences over time. Policies that give people greater material freedom to have children can thus be very consequential in the long term.

If governments fail to enact these policies, and if, indeed, these policies fail to encourage a broader rise in fertility, the world will simply become more unequal. Richer families and richer countries will gain greater weight in the population, while poorer families and poorer countries dwindle and weaken. These shifts will create political tensions, as shrinking populations will add to their relative poverty the desperate sense that they have no demographic future. Eastern Germany offers a preview. Since reunification, its young people (above all, its young women) have left for western Germany, its towns have emptied and aged, and its voters have turned to the parties at both extremes of the political spectrum. Many countries in the world are about to become eastern Germany, but few of them will have a western Germany to pay the bills. Demographers often suggest that the world is united by the crash in fertility rates. In truth, demographic decline will likely divide the world even further.
